ASTANA – As climate change fuels increasingly intense heat waves, staying safe in extreme temperatures has become a growing concern across Kazakhstan. This summer, temperatures have climbed above 40 degrees Celsius in several regions, testing both people’s endurance and public health systems.
Photo credit: AI-generated image/ The Astana Times
While modern households rely on air conditioners and fans, Kazakhstan’s nomadic ancestors developed practical ways to stay cool long before electricity. According to a candidate of historical sciences Saltanat Asanova, many of these centuries-old practices remain relevant today.
“Traditional culture, livelihoods and daily life were always closely connected to the natural environment and its changes. People were prepared for both cold and heat,” Asanova told The Astana Times.
Saltanat Asanova, a candidate of historical sciences. Photo credit: Asanova’s personal archieve
For nomadic herders, extreme summer heat was rarely a major problem because they moved with the seasons.
“Nomads who migrated year-round spent summers in cooler areas, either farther north or in high mountain pastures. Moving livestock to alpine grazing lands was the primary way to escape the summer heat. Even on the hottest days, temperatures in the mountains remain significantly lower than in the steppe,” Asanova said.
Daily routines also followed the rhythm of the sun. Work began at dawn, paused during the hottest midday hours and resumed in the evening as temperatures dropped.
“Most household and pastoral work was completed after sunset, when the heat subsided,” she said.
The science behind a cooler yurt
The yurt, the traditional portable dwelling of Kazakh nomads, played a crucial role in keeping families cool.
According to Asanova, the yurt’s design created constant natural airflow. The shanyrak, the circular opening at the top of the roof, was left open during the day, allowing hot air to rise and escape while cooler air remained inside.
To maximize ventilation, yurts were carefully positioned according to prevailing winds. Although entrances traditionally faced southeast, their orientation could be adjusted depending on local wind conditions. Lifting the edges of the felt covering allowed air to circulate freely through the structure.
“When temperatures became especially high, the side felt coverings were removed entirely, leaving only the wooden lattice frame and reed mats. The small gaps between the reeds created excellent ventilation, helping maintain a comfortable indoor temperature without any additional cooling devices,” Asanova said.
Historical accounts by travelers who visited the Kazakh steppe during the summer describe yurts as being noticeably cooler than the outside air.
The felt roof continued to protect residents from direct sunlight.
“Felt has unique insulating properties. It retains warmth in winter while preventing solar heat from penetrating the dwelling during summer,” Asanova said.
Dressing for the heat
Despite the high temperatures, Kazakhs traditionally wore long, loose-fitting clothing rather than exposing their skin.
“It may seem paradoxical, but the hotter it became, the more layers people wore. Quilted robes provided better protection from the sun than lightweight clothing or bare skin. Like felt, multiple layers acted as insulation against overheating,” Asanova said.
She noted that headwear was equally essential.
“Felt hats effectively protected the head from the scorching sun while preventing excessive heat exposure,” she said.
Summer diet
Seasonal eating also helped people cope with the heat.
“During summer, meat was consumed only rarely. The diet consisted primarily of dairy products such as kymyz, airan, shubat, and milk-based kozhe, a traditional grain-and-milk soup,” Asanova said.
Drinks were stored in leather containers known as burdyuks, whose natural materials allowed air circulation while keeping liquids cool. Wooden tubs and clay vessels were also commonly used.
“Natural materials help maintain a relatively stable temperature regardless of the weather. For the same reason, water was traditionally stored in clay containers or leather bags,” she said.
Asanova noted that although tea remained an expensive imported commodity, both nomadic and settled communities embraced an unusual practice: drinking hot tea during hot weather.
“They followed one principle: the hotter the weather, the hotter the drink. People avoided cold water because they believed it disrupted the body’s natural heat regulation and made the heat feel even more intense. Instead, they drank hot green tea, which helps the body adapt to high temperatures and promotes natural cooling,” she said.
Modern medical advice
As heat waves become more frequent across Kazakhstan, general practitioner Malika Muratbekova said traditional advice on coping with extreme temperatures remains relevant, including avoiding excessive consumption of ice-cold water, especially during meals.
“Very cold liquids can slow digestion. The body has to expend extra energy warming the stomach, which can leave a person feeling even more fatigued,” Muratbekova said in an interview with The Astana Times.
She recommends drinking water in small amounts throughout the day, avoiding sugary soft drinks, and wearing loose-fitting, light-colored clothing made from natural or cooling fabrics with ultraviolet protection.
Muratbekova also advised protecting the head with a hat and cooling the body gradually.
“You can place a cooling towel or damp cloth around your neck. Portable fans are also becoming increasingly common. Taking a cool shower, using a spray bottle or damp cloth to moisten the skin can help lower body temperature. However, avoid ice-cold showers because a sudden drop in temperature can place unnecessary stress on the body,” she said.

President Lee Jae Myung instructed the government Thursday to mobilize all of its resources to minimize damage from a record-breaking heat wave gripping the nation.
Lee issued the order at a meeting with relevant ministers and heads of local governments as temperatures climbed to near 40 C in many parts of the country, with the southeastern city of Yangsan posting the highest recorded temperature of 42.5 C on Sunday.
Thousands of people had visited hospitals and 21 people had died from heat-related illnesses as of Wednesday, according to health authorities.
"The heat wave is highly likely to continue for some time, so the government must with exceptional resolve activate a comprehensive response system until the heat wave eases," Lee said at the meeting at the government complex.
"I ask you to fully mobilize all administrative powers so that the damage to the people from the heat wave and the drought can be minimized."
Lee gave instructions to devise measures to respond to extreme weather, look after senior citizens living alone and shanty town residents, ensure that breaks are implemented at outdoor worksites during the hottest hours, and prevent damage to livestock and crops.

Country diary: Even in a heatwave, signs of last winter storms still linger
South Devon: On holiday in deeply familiar places, we swim fully clothed, snack on overhanging cherries and see the fallen Teignmouth pier
The West Country unrolls down the M4, then M5, under the kind of vintage-yellow hue produced by 35mm camera film where the light’s leaked in. Many fields have been harvested as early as we’ve ever witnessed on this deeply familiar route. Burnt black patches remind us just how flammable the countryside is.
We are exploring places we’ve only passed through before, via a farm-stay in a shepherd’s hut at West Town Farm, Ide. Our parking instructions urge us to allow the farmer to pass in her tractor. The gender reveal is so refreshing I want to cheer. Tenant Kate Sharp farms Hereford-cross beef cattle, Devon closewool and Exmoor horn sheep, as well as some lively Oxford sandy and black pigs, red as the Devon soil itself.
The organic farm, long-established by semi-retiree Andy Bragg, is so close to Exeter, we walk in one day, snacking along the way on cherries and plums overhanging the paths. We spend another day walking the salt-sprayed wall between the sea and railway at Dawlish Warren, which previously I’ve only ever seen, pressed against the window of a Great Western train. Even as we swelter in the heatwave, the destruction caused by winter storms is still visible; Teignmouth’s Great Pier end, collapsed into the sea.
At 20th-century Castle Drogo, we trek towards Sharp Tor, crossing Piddledown Common, where zigzags of bracken leaves suggest basking adders. The heat-shimmered views of Fingle Woods above the Teign Gorge are breathtaking. When we reach the coppery-clear water of the Teign itself, we sink into it, fully-clad, our clothes billowing around us.
When we must leave, it is from a town farm to Village Farm, and its new festival on the fields high above the sea at East Portlemouth. We must squeeze down the narrowest Devon lanes to reach our accommodation (the road along Slapton Sands having been washed away during those same winter storms).
But before we do, the clifftop marquees, sea and sunset are like a painting. Smoke particles from Canadian wildfires, thousands of miles away, scatter the light’s blue wavelengths to show us a halogen-hot red sun. We move like we’re in a dream; all is, briefly, very beautiful.

A Stanford Medicine-developed app shows that older adults’ geographic movements — also known as their life-space mobility — shrink in extreme heat that makes leaving the house difficult.
For some, the hot late summer months can be a season of expansion — sunny afternoon trips to the pool or beach, outdoor concerts and festivals.
But as the planet warms and extreme heat waves become more common in the late summer months, at least one group of people seems to be limiting their movements: older Americans.
A new phone app developed by researchers at Stanford Medicine revealed that older adults across the country constrict their range outside the home when daily average temperatures climb above 84 degrees Fahrenheit. That finding means more than just a missed summer outing, the researchers say — life-space mobility, a measure of how far people travel outside their home on a daily basis, is strongly correlated with overall health in older adults. Their findings were published recently in the journal Innovation in Aging.
“Life-space is a really integrative measure of health,” said Michelle Odden, PhD, an associate professor of epidemiology. “We were interested in measuring it objectively with people’s mobile phones, which even many older adults carry with them every day.”
How far and how often older adults travel outside the home is an indicator of how much they are socializing, how much they’re exercising, and how much they’re engaging with their communities through work, volunteering or attending religious services; all these activities are known to correlate with healthy aging and longer lifespans.
Michelle Odden
An app for mobility
Traditionally, life-space mobility has been measured with questionnaires that ask older adults to recall how many times in the previous week they left their house, their neighborhood, and their town. But studies that rely on recall after the fact may not capture the full picture of a person’s movement.
Annabel Tan, PhD, MPH, a data scientist at Stanford Medicine and former doctoral student in Odden’s lab, and her colleagues built an iPhone app called Cardinal LifeSpace that captures GPS positioning and user-reported data to objectively track older adults’ life-space mobility.
“Older adults are often a forgotten population,” Tan said. “This app could be a tool to help figure out how we should plan for their health.”
The researchers recruited older adults from across the U.S. who were part of a large ongoing study headquartered at the University of Alabama at Birmingham to assess stroke risk factors in Black and white adults. Tan and her colleagues wanted to test the feasibility of their app to capture life-space mobility and to ask whether older adults’ movements outside their home varied with temperature.
Their study tracked the movements of 82 adults with an average age of 74.5 over the course of two weeks in summer, fall or winter. The researchers looked at the geographical areas the older adults traveled during each day, as well as the farthest distance they traveled from their homes.
They found that once the daily average temperature hit 84 degrees Fahrenheit, that 2D space started shrinking. The study participants reduced the area they ventured outside the house by nearly two-thirds of a square mile for every degree the daily average temperature rose above 84 degrees.
“This is the first study to show that higher temperatures can constrict life-space,” Odden said. “That could result in less social engagement, less physical activity, and less time spent in the community — all of those things we know are important for healthy aging.”
Previous studies in other countries, mostly in Scandinavian countries, used questionnaires to address how life-space mobility in older adults correlates with temperature and did not find this connection. But those studies did not include the level of extreme summer temperatures that are now felt in many parts of the U.S.
As we age, our bodies’ ability to regulate internal temperatures decreases. Older adults can’t cool themselves down when it’s hot or warm themselves up when it’s cold like they used to. On hot days, that means higher risk of heat stroke or heat exhaustion.
Add in chronic conditions like diabetes or heart disease — also both more prevalent in older adults — and that temperature regulation becomes even more dysfunctional. Extreme heat itself can also increase the risk of heart attacks and strokes, especially in older adults.
Older adults also have a blunted sense of thirst, meaning they are more likely to become dehydrated, especially on hot days. Making sure to get in those eight to 10 cups of water daily is especially important for folks over 65, Odden said.
Policy considerations
Because extreme heat poses danger to the aging population, the researchers’ findings shouldn’t be interpreted to mean that older adults should push themselves to get out for a sweltering hike when temperatures climb, Tan and Odden said. Rather, it’s a message for policy makers and city planners to consider public infrastructure like air-conditioned community centers to keep aging populations healthy while also allowing for social and physical engagement.
Lower-income areas need special attention when it comes to staying healthy in the heat, Tan said, because residents there are less likely to have air conditioning and, in cities, poorer neighborhoods are actually hotter than wealthier ones due to the lack of green spaces.
“It could be as simple as planting more trees in certain areas,” Tan said.
Taking a few days off from walks with your neighbors or your volunteer gig when the thermostat climbs isn’t going to make a big health difference on an individual basis. But climate change is bringing us more frequent and longer heat waves, so that restricted activity could eventually add up to a significant difference on a population-wide level.
“If you disrupt healthy habits, that can shift the trajectory slowly over time to less physical activity, less social engagement, less cognitive stimulation,” Odden said. “And this is something that policy makers need to pay attention to and create alternative resources for older adults as we deal with a warming climate.”

An orange alert means “Be Prepared” for heavy to very heavy rain (typically 115.6 mm to 204.4 mm in 24 hrs) while a yellow alert means “Be Aware” (typically 64.5 mm to 115.5 mm in 24 hrs)
Delhi continued to receive light to moderate rainfall on Thursday with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issuing an ‘orange alert’ today and ‘yellow alert’ for Friday.
An orange rainfall warning means “Be Prepared” for heavy to very heavy rain (typically 115.6 mm to 204.4 mm in 24 hours) while a yellow rainfall warning means “Be Aware” (typically 64.5 mm to 115.5 mm in 24 hours).
Multiple parts of Delhi received light showers late Wednesday night and early Thursday morning. From 11:30pm on Wednesday to 8:30am on Thursday, Palam recorded the highest rainfall at 23.8mm, followed by Naraina 23.5mm, and Janakpuri at 17.5mm.
During the same period, Pusa recorded 6.5mm, followed by Chhatarpur at 4.5mm, and Mayur Vihar at 3.5mm. Safdarjung, the city’s base station for weather, recorded 3.1mm of rainfall during the same period.
At around 9:15am, the IMD issued a red alert for Shahdara, east, south east, central, and south Delhi, most parts of north east, central, along with parts of west, north west, and north Delhi, predicting heavy rain with thunderstorms and lightning in the same parts.
Multiple spells of very light to light rain at most places with moderate rain at a few places during the early morning to noon is predicted for Friday, while another spell of very light to light rain is likely towards evening or night.
The IMD categorizes rainfall up to 15.5mm as light, between 15.6mm to 64.4mm as ‘moderate’, between 64.5mm to 115.5mm as ‘heavy’, and between 115.6mm to 204.4mm as ‘very heavy’.
Experts have stated that the increased rain over the past few days, after a number of days with no significant rain, was due to the monsoon trough returning to be positioned over northern India.
“The rains have picked up across Delhi as the excess of the monsoon trough that was over central and western India has started to move back to its position over the foothills of the Himalayas. Such scattered rain seen today is likely to be seen today as well, with only around 30% to 60% of NCR seeing strong showers, while other areas get light rain or remain completely dry. In the coming two weeks, NCR is likely to continue seeing days like today, with a few days with heavy rains in some parts of the region,” said Ashwary Tiwari, founder of Indiametsky weather.
AQI ‘satisfactory’
The city’s air quality index (AQI) was recorded at 80 around 11:05am, in the “satisfactory” category.
Due to the rain, the maximum temperature is expected to be between 31°C to 33°C, rising to 33°C to 35°C on Saturday. Thursday’s minimum temperature was recorded at 25.6°C.

‘Life-saving services’: Medford cooling shelter open through Friday as heat spikes
Published 1:27 pm Wednesday, August 5, 2026
The shelter provides air conditioning, water and other resources; community members, ‘non-aggressive’ pets welcome
With high temperatures expected to be over 100 degrees for much of this week, Medford’s severe weather shelter will be open from noon to 8 p.m. through Friday to provide an escape from the potentially dangerous heat wave outside.
Located at 332 W. 6th Street in Medford, the shelter is operated by nonprofit ACCESS, a Community Action Agency of Jackson County. It offers free resources from air conditioning and water to resource navigation for those in need of housing.
“It’s probably one of the most critical, life-saving services that can be provided to our community’s most vulnerable residents,” said Melanie Doshier, ACCESS chief program officer. “I could go on and on about the success stories that we’ve had with community members who have utilized our severe weather shelter and the relationship that we’ve been able to build with them over time.”
ACCESS coordinates with the city of Medford when deciding when to open the shelter, which is used in scenarios such as extreme heat and cold, and hazardous smoke indexes.
Savannah Schmidt, who was waiting outside the shelter late afternoon on Tuesday, said she had only been there once before, but it was “excellent.” However, she said the city should have more resources available for those dealing with the heat wave.
“I don’t think it’s a solution that they should lean on,” she said. “The City of Medford shouldn’t lean on (the shelter) with the capacity of 74 people.”
Email newsletter signup
Schmidt said she has been homeless for “a few months.”
“It’s not just like people that are making bad decisions,” she said. “It’s really easy to (become) homeless here.”
Doshier said the shelter’s funding includes state and federal funds. However, it relies heavily on volunteers when it is open.
“It is a shelter that is staffed by volunteers, as well as other ACCESS staff members and security that have other full-time jobs,” she said. “And so, (we’re) making sure that we are utilizing the best resources in the best place for the most impact.”
Although the shelter is scheduled to close at 8 p.m. during its open days this week, it can be used as an overnight shelter during the winter when cold temperatures become a safety risk, or if smoke levels become hazardous during the summer.
Doshier said that depending on what supplies are available, the shelter supplies those in need with food, dry storage, emergency kits, popsicles on hot days, sanitation supplies and lightly-used clothing and shoes.
Those interested in donating volunteer hours or supplies to the shelter or other ACCESS services can visit accesshelps.org/get-involved/. For updates on the cooling shelter via text notification, text MED4SHELTERS to 888777.
“ACCESS is full of staff members and volunteers and board members, and everybody that contributes to our mission is really dedicated to positive outcomes,” Doshier said. “And we couldn’t do it without everybody doing their part.”
The organization celebrated its 50th anniversary in July. Doshier said ACCESS started coordinating with the city regarding the severe weather shelter in 2020 when Covid-19 affected other volunteer efforts. ACCESS became the operator of the shelter in 2022.
Doshier said the number of people visiting the shelter “varies drastically” on open days. “In the summer, we’ve seen 20 people visit the shelter, and then there’s days that we’ve seen 70 people visit the shelter.
“The numbers fluctuate,” she said, “but we want to make sure that we are open for those that need it.”
Doshier said that the shelter primarily serves those without homes, but its free resources are open to any community members, such as those without air conditioning and people struggling to get out of the heat. The shelter also welcomes “non-aggressive” pets.

Yet more rinse-and-repeat flood warnings were posted for Philadelphia and portions of adjacent counties Wednesday as more downpours oozed through the region.
And don’t be surprised if more pop up later in the week, as the atmosphere will remain thickened with so much skin-clinging water vapor that “it’s not going to take much” to turn on the faucets, said Michael Silva, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Mount Holly.
One indicator of the atmospheric saturation: The weather service has posted a heat advisory for Thursday as heat indexes could rise to 100 or better — even though temperatures won’t get much past 90. That is all about the humidity in what could be the start of a more muggy wave, as opposed to a traditional heat wave.
The moisture in the air on Wednesday was such that the rain, which began around lunchtime, ended up being more ferocious than expected.
“Before work, I was about to go out twice for walks,” Silva said. “Then I looked at the radar.”
The heavy rains were wrung out along a narrow corridor cutting through the city, and they generated widespread traffic disruptions during the afternoon.
The weather service said that 1.23 inches of rain had been measured at Philadelphia International Airport, just between noon and 1 p.m. More than 2 inches fell upon parts of Bucks County.
Road flooding was widespread in Philly, Bucks County, and South Jersey.
Among the highways affected were the Schuylkill Expressway in the Point Breeze area; I-95 in Eastwick, at the Platt Bridge, and in the Croydon, Bucks County, area, where the warning was extended until 6:15 p.m.; and Route 130 in Burlington County.
The rains were getting juice from a rich pulse of moisture from the South, said Mike Gorse, a meteorologist at the weather service’s Mount Holly office.
What’s more, these types of threats may be a “repeated thing” later in the week, he added, echoing Silva’s comment, with showers in the forecast again for Thursday night and Friday as the region is stuck in another sultry air mass.
The recent rains represent quite a reversal of fortune for the region and the entire state of New Jersey.
After 16 consecutive months of below-normal precipitation in Philly, officially close to 10 inches of rain has been measured since July 1, and recent rains have set off rashes of flood warnings, including on Sunday.
July’s total, 7.03 inches, was 2.65 inches above normal.
Still, water levels along the Schuylkill in Norristown and the Delaware River at Trenton have remained relatively low, the result of all that antecedent dryness.
However, flashier creeks, such as the Neshaminy, in Bucks County, are prone to slosh over in downpours, said Sarah Johnson, the weather service’s warning coordination meteorologist in Mount Holly.
While Chester County and all of New Jersey remain under drought warnings, the recent turn to wetness may have some staying power, she said.
According to the weather service’s Middle Atlantic River Forecast Center, which relies on networks of observations in each county, rainfall in all 21 counties in New Jersey has been well above normal in the 60-day period that ended on Tuesday.
On the Pennsylvania side, rainfall was at or above normal in Philly and its neighboring counties — including Chester County, where the 9.17-inch total was 113% of normal.
The federal Climate Prediction Center’s longer-term outlooks see chances favoring above-normal precipitation from next Tuesday through Aug. 19.
